newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba comments revive rate cut speculation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba comments revive rate cut speculation.

text.p: The Bundesbank revived hopes for lower German interest rates on Friday as two of its council members hinted policy might yet be eased, only two days after policy makers had quashed all rate-cut speculation.

Speaking at separate events, the central bank's chief economist, Otmar Issing, and council member Ernst Welteke stressed there was no need to cut rates now but held out hope that the bank could consider a further easing.

Issing, whose comments in a German television interview on Wednesday had ended financial market hopes for lower rates, was asked in Brussels if he meant to rule out any rate cuts forever. He responded: "Of course not. There is never an end."
Meanwhile, Welteke told reporters in Frankfurt that in the medium term, "a repo cut is still possible depending on developments."
The remarks prompted a sharp jump in German bonds and stocks and elsewhere in Europe as speculation spread that the Bundesbank might still be ready to lower yields and fan economic growth.
"The market is incredibly nervous right now," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at UBS. "A segment of the market saw these comments and decided it had to jump on the bandwagon."
Two days ago Issing said: "Key rates are at a historic low here and nothing more is to be expected or necessary."

That remark, combined with the bank's decision to keep rates on hold at its regular council meeting on Thursday, led many to believe that with the economy on the mend, it had decided not to lower rates any further in the current business cycle.
The discount rate already stands at a historic low of 2.5 percent, the emergency Lombard lending facility at 4.5 percent and the securities repurchase rate (repo) at 3.00 percent.
Some analysts said the latest comments were a deliberate move to soften the impact of Issing's strong words on Wednesday.

Indeed, Welteke, unusually speaking for another member of the Bundesbank council, said he did not think Issing intended "with his little comment to take interest rate speculation out of the market for all time."
Harry Thapar, analyst at MCM YieldWatch in London, said that remark showed the Bundesbank was trying to at least leave the door open to further rate cuts.
"Issing's tone on Wednesday was very aggressive. They wanted to calm things," he said.
Others, however, said the remarks were only stating the obvious and that nervous financial markets, eager to jump on latest headline, were overstating Bundesbank intentions.
"Issing has said the same thing several times in recent weeks," Fahrinkrug said. "The market has lost its orientation and in these situations, the smallest comments will move it."
